title: Medicare Will Soon Cover Weight Loss Drugs—But There's a Catch!
summary: Have you heard about those medicines that help people lose weight, like Wegovy or Zepbound? They can be super expensive—sometimes hundreds of dollars a month! But here's some big news: starting in July 2026, a new Medicare program called the GLP-1 Bridge will let some people get these drugs for just $50 a month. That's a huge discount. But, like a video game with tricky rules, there are catches. First, you must have Medicare Part D (that's the part that covers prescription drugs). Second, your doctor has to say you need it based on your weight and health. For example, if your body mass index, or BMI, is 35 or higher, you automatically qualify. If it's 27 or higher and you have heart disease or prediabetes, you might qualify too. Now, here's the twist: the $50 you pay doesn't count toward your Part D deductible or the $2,100 yearly cap on drug costs. That means you could still pay a lot for other medicines. Also, this Bridge program is only a pilot—it ends in December 2027. What happens after that? Nobody knows yet. Plus, studies show that many people who stop taking these drugs gain the weight back. So, if the program ends and you can't afford the full price, you might lose the progress you made. Another bummer: if you get Extra Help (a low-income subsidy), you can't use it for these drugs. For someone living on a small Social Security check, even $50 a month can be tough. Still, for many, this is a chance to try a treatment that was out of reach. Just make sure you understand the fine print before you jump in!
why_it_matters: If your grandparents or relatives rely on Medicare, this could help them afford a medicine that might keep them healthier and more active.

background_read: Obesity affects millions of Americans and can lead to heart disease and diabetes. For years, Medicare did not cover weight loss drugs because they were seen as lifestyle medicines, not treatments for disease. In 2024, new rules allowed Medicare to consider covering them if used for obesity-related health conditions. The GLP-1 Bridge program is a limited trial to see if making these drugs affordable improves health and saves money.
Article_Structure: WHO: People with Medicare Part D who have a high BMI or related health conditions like heart disease or prediabetes
WHAT: The GLP-1 Bridge program will provide weight-loss drugs for $50 a month, but the payment doesn't count toward deductibles and the pilot ends in December 2027
WHERE: Across the United States for those enrolled in Medicare
WHY: To test whether making these expensive drugs affordable improves people's health, while managing costs and studying what happens when coverage stops

perspectives.description: Many people who couldn't afford $1,000-a-month weight loss drugs now have a chance to try them, which could improve health and quality of life.
The $50 cost might still be too much for seniors on a fixed income, and the program ends in 2027—if people can't pay full price then, they may regain the weight, creating a tough cycle.
The pilot program will gather data on whether covering these drugs actually reduces other health costs, which could influence future Medicare decisions.
